title: Spiral galaxy NGC 4945
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 4945, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope at La Silla, Chile
celestial: NGC 4945 · constellation Centaurus · about 13 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #91 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Bright pink patches mark HII regions, places where stars are actively forming, across this edge-on galaxy. It is NGC 4945, about 13 million light-years away in the constellation Centaurus, the Centaur, pictured with the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope at La Silla.

Observations suggest that NGC 4945 is a spiral resembling the Milky Way, with glowing, swirling arms and a central bar. Because we see it edge-on, though, those arms are not laid out flat before us as they would be in a face-on view.

One difference stands out. NGC 4945 has a brighter center that likely hosts a supermassive black hole, thought to be swallowing large amounts of matter and hurling energy out into space. The image was assembled from five filter bands (B, V, R, H-alpha and S II), and the field of view measures 30 by 30 arcminutes.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (21.96 x 21.96 arcminutes) and distance (13 million light years), the frame spans roughly 83,000 × 83,000 light-years. Its light set out about 13 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope observed in five visible bands, including hydrogen-alpha and sulfur (S II) filters. Star-forming regions appear pink, but the full mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Long camera exposures gather much more light than the eye can.
